seasons.review_body: Adapted from Jornn Lier Horst's novels The Caveman and The Hunting Dogs, the debut season of Wisting arrived on Viaplay and TV3 in April 2019 with Sven Nordin anchoring the series as William Wisting - a detective whose quiet authority never tips into cliche. The season pulls off a structural gambit most Nordic noirs avoid: it runs a Norwegian cold case investigation alongside a live FBI hunt, with Carrie-Anne Moss as Special Agent Maggie Griffin providing genuine transatlantic tension rather than an obvious American hook. Critics at Rotten Tomatoes gave the season 81 percent from 4 reviews. Dorothy Rabinowitz in the Wall Street Journal called every episode alive. Euan Ferguson in the Observer went further, calling it the best Nordic noir ever made. Premiere viewership broke Viaplay streaming records with over 250,000 viewers per episode across platforms.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# Wisting S1E1: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The television stays on. That is the first smart cruelty of Wisting’s opener. A dead man sits in his armchair long enough for the room to become a clock, long enough for the set to keep talking to nobody, long enough for **Hammer** to put a number on the silence: three months. The episode’s thesis is built right there. This is a procedural about evidence, but its force comes from delay. A body can be present and still be unidentified. A suspect can be named and still be uncertain. A case can begin with stillness and grow more frightening as facts arrive.

## The Corpse Is a Clock

The opening movement is patient in a way most crime pilots fear. Before the investigation starts moving, the episode lets vacancy do the work. The early on-screen promise of self-realization sits beside the later image of **Viggo Hansen** mummifying in his chair, and the contrast is harsh without being decorated. A course on looking after yourself, then a man nobody seems to have found for months. The show does not need a speech about loneliness. It has a television left on too long.

That choice gives the episode its strongest procedural hook. Hammer’s line of inquiry around the TV is not decorative. It turns a grim visual into a time window, then into a lead. The channel matters because the room has been performing normal life after life has stopped. BollyAI’s read: the hour works best when it treats objects as witnesses. A chair, a screen, a plastic bag, a biblical ship, an old well. None of them explain themselves. The investigators have to make them talk.

The restraint also helps the tone. The dossier notes long quiet gaps before and around the early case work, and that rhythm matters. The pilot opens like a room being entered carefully. That confidence earns the later urgency because the show has first made the audience sit with the dead air. It gives the case a physical temperature. Cold. Stale. Undisturbed for too long.

The risk with this kind of patience is drift. Wisting mostly avoids it because the stillness keeps producing questions. Who was this man to the people around him? How does someone vanish while remaining in his own living room? Why does the ordinary evidence feel so wrong? The episode does not rush to dignify the death with meaning. It lets neglect hang over the scene first, which makes the procedural work feel less abstract once it begins.

## Secrecy Becomes the First Suspect

Once the body is found, the immediate concern is information control. The investigators decide to announce only that a body was found until identity is known. Later, the operational warning tightens the walls further: no town chatter, no home discussion, no press. The case depends on discovering facts and controlling their circulation. Every detail has weight because every detail can leak.

That is where the hour begins to build friction around **Line Wisting**. The dossier frames her contradiction cleanly: she wants reporting access and stays close to the investigation, gaining keys and later appearing in connection with missing-woman leads. That is a useful pressure point for a first episode because it turns procedure into family and media tension without requiring melodrama. The police need silence. Line needs proximity. The show plants that conflict early enough to matter, then leaves it alive.

The weakness is that this section is more promising than piercing. The secrecy rules are clear, but their emotional cost is still mostly theoretical in this hour. The show tells the audience what cannot be said and where it cannot be said. It has not yet made the silence hurt beyond case mechanics. For a premiere, that is acceptable. For the season to grow teeth, that boundary needs to cut someone personally.

Line’s position matters because she is not a random civilian with inconvenient curiosity. She has access, professional hunger, and family proximity to the investigation. The episode understands the problem but has not yet pushed it into danger. That may be deliberate. A first episode can set a fuse without lighting it. Still, the Line material needs sharper consequence soon, because the procedural side is already carrying enough weight to expose any soft personal drama around it.

## A Fingerprint Is Not a Man

The first major acceleration comes through **Alfheim**’s report: fingerprints on a plastic bag connect the investigation to **Robert Godwin**, a man wanted in the US. It is a classic procedural jolt, and the episode stages it with a productive contradiction. The evidence gives the team a name, while the case refuses to let that name become certainty too quickly. The dossier’s central contradiction around Alfheim is the episode in miniature: evidence-based confidence lands beside the warning that they cannot be completely sure.

That is good crime writing because it keeps the clue from becoming a shortcut. A weaker pilot would treat the fingerprint as a solved identity and move on. Wisting uses it as a door into a larger confusion. If Godwin is connected to the scene, is he the dead man, the killer, a ghost identity, or some uglier combination? The answer shifts again when the biblical ship clue leads to a missing elderly North American renter, and then the DNA report identifies the body as **Peter Crabb**. In one movement, the investigation goes from a wanted man to a dead man to the space between them.

The reframe is the hour’s cleanest turn. Godwin’s name arrives with international weight. Crabb’s identification pulls the story back to the chair, the house, the body. The episode understands that a procedural twist lands harder when it changes the question instead of merely adding another one. After the DNA result, the case pivots from identification to relationship. How does Crabb connect to Godwin, and what kind of hiding has been happening in Norway?

This is also where the premiere shows discipline. It does not overplay the international angle as instant scale. The US connection matters, but the episode keeps returning to concrete evidence. Fingerprints. A renter. A body. DNA. The case widens through procedure, which makes the widening feel earned. Godwin is a frightening name because the evidence is messy, not because the show keeps telling the audience to be frightened.

## The Wells Turn the Case Vertical

The late pivot to missing young women gives the premiere its darkest expansion. The instruction to check open cases going back twenty years, with wells noted as hiding places, changes the physical imagination of the case. Until then, the episode is built around surfaces: a living room, a bag, fingerprints, a rented house. The wells send the investigation downward. The geography of the crime becomes older, colder, and more buried.

This is where the Godwin thread becomes more than a fugitive alert. The possibility that his method of hiding victims in old wells has translated into the Norway case gives the episode its season engine. It also reframes the early quiet. That dead living room was not an isolated grotesque image. It may be the visible edge of something hidden for years.

The mention of **Ellen Robekk**, the missing colleague’s niece, sharpens that expansion by giving the open loop a name. The episode does not need to answer whether she is alive or among the well remains. It only has to make the question feel urgent, and it does. The case list dating back two decades prevents the plot from narrowing into one dead body and one wanted American. BollyAI’s read: this is the hour’s best structural move. It starts with a corpse nobody found for three months, then suggests an entire landscape where people may have disappeared for much longer.

The wells also give the episode a stronger horror texture without breaking its procedural frame. They are practical hiding places, which is the point. The idea is awful because it is plain. A body can be lowered out of sight. A disappearance can become geography. The show does not need a baroque killer signature when an old well carries that much dread.

This final expansion is the reason the opener works as a season starter rather than a contained case. The dead man in the chair is still central, but he is no longer the outer edge of the story. He becomes an entry point. The hour’s patience pays off because the case has moved from one sealed room to a wider map without losing the chill of the first image.

## The Verdict

Wisting’s first episode is a controlled procedural opener with one excellent instinct: it lets uncertainty remain useful. The body in the chair, the plastic-bag fingerprints, the Peter Crabb DNA result, and the wells do not stack as random clues. They keep changing the shape of the central question. The hour is less successful when its secrecy conflict stays at the level of rules and access, especially around Line, but the craft is sturdy enough to make that feel like a planted fuse. BollyAI’s score: 7.4/10. As a season starter, it earns its slot by building a case that can widen while holding onto the dead room that began it.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A restrained opener turns one dead room into a widening case, with strong clues and slightly undercooked personal friction.

bollymeter.basis: Condensed to 4 episodes, Season 2 maintains the procedural quality but loses the sprawl that made Season 1 exceptional. Based on The Inner Darkness.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 (adapting Horst's The Inner Darkness) aired as a 4-episode run on Viaplay from late December 2021. The compressed format - half the episode count of Season 1 - means the investigation moves faster but breathes less. Sven Nordin remains the moral gravity of the series, and the Larvik winter landscape continues to do atmospheric work that most crime dramas spend a budget trying to manufacture. Carrie-Anne Moss returns, keeping the FBI thread alive. The season functions as a satisfying case-closed chapter rather than an expansion of the first season's ambitions.
seasons.season_over_season: Shorter and tighter than Season 1, Season 2 trades the first season's slow-burn sprawl for a focused 4-episode case - effective but narrower in scope.

seasons.review_body: Season 3, based on Horst's The Hunting Dogs novel, continued the 4-episode format that the series adopted after its debut season. The story focuses on a cold case that implicates figures inside the police force - a structural choice that raises the stakes for Wisting personally. The compact runtime serves this more introspective arc well, keeping the investigation taut without overstaying its welcome.
seasons.season_over_season: Turns the procedural lens inward as Season 3 implicates law enforcement itself, adding personal cost to what had been Wisting's professional mission.

seasons.review_body: Season 4 arrived in March 2024 adapting Horst's A Question of Guilt, continuing the compressed 4-episode structure that became the series' post-debut format. BBC iPlayer coverage described the writing as having genius-level craft, and the season drew strong online attention as the final arc of the series began to take shape. The Larvik setting and Nordin's performance remain the anchors.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 4 deepens the personal dimension of Wisting's cases as the series builds toward its conclusion.

seasons.review_body: The fifth and final season aired in September 2024 on Viaplay, with Sven Nordin confirming it as his farewell to the Wisting role. Shelley Conn of Bridgerton guest-starred, broadening the series' international dimension for the final run. The season closes out the five-year arc that began with the FBI crossover in 2019 - a proper send-off for a procedural that, at its peak, held the Nordic noir crown.
seasons.season_over_season: The series finale season delivers a proper send-off for Nordin's Wisting, trading procedural tension for character resolution after five seasons.
